Soccer is the world’s most popular sport with billions (yes, billions) of fans worldwide. content:Speaker user says: Reflect on the current state of international politics and nationalism in light of the lessons learned from past global wars.
Generate according to: Elizabeth Morgan | 100 years later, have we learnt?
My father was 10 years old when the First World War, the Great War, the war to end all wars, started on July 28, 1914. He was 14 when it ended on November 11, 1918. He was 35 when the Second World War, the sequel, started.
I thus grew up with many stories about the Jamaican experience in both wars and developed a great interest in them. I actually visited Flanders in Belgium in 2007 and saw the red poppies, symbol of the war and remembrance, growing in the fields where trenches were still being uncovered with bodies inside.
On Armistice Day, today, the world, including Jamaica, will commemorate the 100th anniversary of the end of World War I. There will be major ceremonies in Europe. Here in Jamaica, there will be the annual wreath-laying at the Cenotaph.
There are monuments here in schools, churches, and town squares in memory of the young Jamaican men who volunteered and made the ultimate sacrifice "for King and country". The WWI commemorations in Jamaica have been low-key. However, I attended a lecture at Up Park Camp and a wonderful concert at Kingston Parish Church. At least these events and the poppies show that we have not forgotten.
In the summer of 1914 when war was declared, after nearly 100 years of relative peace in Europe, including La Belle Epoque, King George V, King of Britain and her Empire (including Jamaica), was quoted as saying, "It is a terrible catastrophe. Please God it will end soon." His prayer was not answered. The "terrible catastrophe" dragged on for four years and demonstrated that man's inhumanity to his fellowman, and, indeed, to animals, knew no bounds.
By the armistice on November 11, 1918, more than 40 million military personnel and civilians had died. This included more than 1,250 men from Jamaica and the British West Indies. A whole generation of young men had been lost. Well in excess of eight million horses, mules, donkeys, and dogs were also sacrificed, along with pigeons, in this "great" war, really a fierce family conflict. Through intermarriage among European royal houses, three of the main combatants were cousins: Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany, King George V of Britain, and Czar Nicholas II of Russia.
Nationalism, ambition, and poor decision-making had led to this reckless venture. Many of the armies were ill-equipped for warfare in the 20th century. They came with weapons and tactics from the 19th century. Leaders were inexperienced and ill-equipped. Men went to war with great enthusiasm, expecting to be home in months, if not weeks. Little did they know of the absolute hell of mud, cold, bombs, gas, mutilation, mental disorder, and death that waited and that months would be years. They came with simmering discontent in their own countries and empires.
It became truly a world war involving directly nearly all the continents of the world and the great empires, including the Ottoman. The United States of America, with the Doughboys, entered the war in 1917. Japan was involved. Others such as Latin America felt the impact indirectly. Many countries can tell of major losses and victories.
Many of us have seen the movies and mini-series about the Somme, Paschendaele, Ypres, Gallipoli, Vimy Ridge - and all was not quiet on the western front. More recently, I recall the film War Horse, commemorating the yeoman service of the horses. Some of the names of politicians, officers, and other participants are also familiar: Winston Churchill, Bernard Montgomery, Louis Mountbatten, Douglas McArthur, George Patton, and Corporal Adolf Hitler, to name a few.
The conflagration ended with the Treaty of Versailles. Europe was in ruins. Empires (Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman) and monarchies (Russia, Germany) would be toppled. The map of Europe and parts of Asia and Africa would be redrawn. New powers would rise - the USA and the Soviet Union. New organisations were created, for example, the League of Nations.
Regrettably, in 21 years, less than a generation, World War II would commence. Nationalism had again reared its ugly head. Many of the players were the same. New stars would also emerge. This four-year catastrophe would end in 1945 with the dropping of the atomic bomb, visiting untold horror on Japan. We had entered the nuclear age of total annihilation. Europe was again in ruins. The map was again redrawn and new organisations such as the United Nations was created.
There was a pledge to build international peace and security. The world, as we know it today, was shaped by the victors: the United States and the other allies, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union (Russia). The United States became a superpower extremely influential in shaping the world order.
Today, we are seeing an attempt to dismantle this world order from an unlikely source. The US president is telling the world that he is a nationalist, an advocate of 'America First'. We are seeing the rise of nationalism in Europe. Let us pray that in this period of the 21st century, history is not about to repeat itself. A reckless and terrible catastrophe in our times would indeed be an apocalypse with unimagined consequences for the human race and the world. Armageddon could be upon us.
Let us also pray that lessons from our past global conflagrations have been learnt and good sense will prevail. I have the feeling, though, that, at this time, my father is not resting well in his grave.
- Elizabeth Morgan is a specialist in international trade policy and international politics. Email feedback to columns@gleanerjm.com. context:The year is 2023. content:Speaker assistant says: Basic Financial Planning: How to Start Planning Your Financial Future

Financial planning is an important aspect of life that everyone should take seriously. The primary goal of financial planning is to help you achieve your financial goals, including short-term, medium-term, and long-term goals. Financial planning also helps you to create a roadmap for achieving your goals based on your current financial situation.

Here’s a how-to guide for basic financial planning:

1. Set Your Financial Goals

The first step towards achieving your financial goals is to set them. These goals can be anything from paying off your debts, saving for a down payment on a house, or investing for your future retirement. Ensure you set clear and achievable goals that can be measured.

2. Assess Your Financial Situation

To achieve your financial goals, you must assess your current financial situation. This will involve examining your cash inflows (wages, salary, and investments) and outflows (expenses, bills, and debts). You can also take stock of your assets, liabilities, and net worth. Knowing your financial situation will help you to identify areas that require improvement.

3. Create a Budget

Now that you know your financial situation and goals, the next step is to create a budget. A budget is a plan that outlines how much money you will spend each month or week. It should be balanced and include your needs and wants. The goal of your budget is to help you manage your cashflow better and save money towards your short-term and long-term goals.

4. Track Your Spending

The next step towards good financial planning is tracking your spending. Tracking your expenses will help you to identify where your money is going each day, week, or month. You can use budgeting apps or spreadsheet software to keep track of your expenses. This will help you make informed decisions on what expenses to cut or increase.

5. Develop a Saving Plan

It is essential to develop a saving plan that aligns with your financial goals. It would help if you decided how much money you will save each month or week towards your short-term and long-term goals. Also, consider opening an emergency fund that can cover at least six months of your living expenses.

6. Pay off Your Debts

Paying off debt should be an integral part of your financial planning. Identify your debts, and create a plan to pay them off incrementally. You can also consider debt consolidation or refinancing your loans to reduce your interest rates.

7. Invest for Your Future

Finally, consider investing your money for your future. Investing can be done through different investment vehicles, including stocks, bonds, and mutual funds. Choose an investment option that aligns with your risk appetite, financial goals, and time horizon.

In conclusion, financial planning is a critical aspect of life that requires commitment and discipline. Ensure you follow these basic steps to take control of your finances, achieve your goals, and secure your financial future. context:Budget is important for prioritizing financial goals.  It’s crucial to create a budget and allocate funds based on your priorities. keywords: financial planning, financial goals, budgeting, saving, debt, investing, financial future tags: budget

content:Speaker assistant says: Step-by-Step Guide to Creating a Personalized Budget and Managing Your Finances Effectively:

1. Assess your current financial situation: Before you start creating a budget, it’s important to have an understanding of your current financial situation. Determine your income, expenses, debts, and savings. This will give you a clear picture of where you stand financially.

2. Set financial goals: Once you’ve assessed your current financial situation, it’s time to set financial goals. Make your goals specific, measurable, and realistic. For example, if you want to save $5,000 this year, break it down into smaller monthly goals.

3. Create a budget: Based on your income, expenses, and financial goals, create a budget. Use a budgeting tool or spreadsheet to make it easier. Allocate a certain amount of money to each category, such as housing, food, transportation, entertainment, and so on. Make sure to include savings as well.

4. Track your spending: To ensure that you’re sticking to your budget, track your spending regularly. Use a budgeting app, spreadsheet, or notebook. Review your spending at the end of each week or month, and see if there’s any room for improvement.

5. Reduce your expenses: Look for ways to reduce your expenses. For example, you can try cutting back on eating out, canceling unnecessary subscriptions, or shopping for deals. You can also negotiate bills or switch to a cheaper provider.

6. Increase your income: Besides reducing your expenses, you can also increase your income. Look for opportunities to earn more, such as taking on a side gig, selling items you no longer need, or asking for a raise at work.

7. Build an emergency fund: Unexpected expenses can happen at any time, so it’s important to have an emergency fund. Set aside a portion of your income each month toward your emergency fund. Aim to have at least three to six months’ worth of living expenses saved up.

8. Pay off debt: The longer you carry debt, the more interest you’ll have to pay. Make a plan to pay off your debt as soon as possible. Focus on paying off high-interest debt first, such as credit card debt.

9. Stay motivated: Managing your finances can be challenging, but it’s important to stay motivated. Keep track of your progress, celebrate your achievements, and learn from your mistakes. Remember your financial goals and keep working toward them.

Common Budgeting Mistakes and How to Avoid Them:

- Not being realistic: Make sure your budget is based on realistic numbers. Don’t underestimate expenses or overestimate income.
- Not including all expenses: Make sure you’re including all your expenses in your budget, such as irregular expenses or occasional expenses.
- Not reviewing your budget regularly: Your budget should be reviewed regularly, especially if your income or expenses change.
- Not adjusting your budget: If you’re consistently overspending in a certain category, adjust your budget accordingly.
- Not sticking to your budget: A budget is only effective if you stick to it. Avoid impulse purchases and stay disciplined.

Resources for Further Assistance:

- Mint: A free budgeting app that helps track and categorize your spending.
- YNAB: A budgeting app that focuses on giving every dollar a job and helps you save for future expenses.
- Personal Capital: A financial tool that tracks your net worth, investments, and retirement savings.
- Dave Ramsey: A financial guru who offers budgeting tips and debt reduction strategies.
- Local non-profit financial counseling agencies: Many non-profit organizations offer free or low-cost financial counseling services. Check with your local community for resources. context:budgeting keywords: budget, financial management, personal finance, saving, debt, expenses, goals, money management tags: debt

content:Speaker assistant says: Creating a successful budget plan can seem daunting, but it's an essential step in achieving financial stability and success. Here's a thorough guide with clear and concise instructions that can help you create a budget plan that works for your unique situation.

Step 1: Identify Your Income and Expenses

Before creating a budget plan, you need to know how much money you have coming in and going out. To do this:

1. Calculate Your Income- Add up all your sources of income for a set period, such as a month. This may include your salary, side hustle income, government benefits, and bonuses.

2. List Your Expenses- Record each expense you have for that set period, including fixed and variable expenses such as rent, mortgage, utilities, groceries, transportation, entertainment, and debt payments.

3. Categorize Your Expenses- Group your expenses into categories such as housing, food, transportation, and entertainment.

Tip: Use a budgeting tool like a spreadsheet or an app to keep track of your income and expenses. It can help you stay organized and save time.

Step 2: Set Financial Goals

Once you know how much money you're making and spending, it's time to set financial goals. Determine what you want to achieve and prioritize these goals. Here are some examples of financial goals:

- Pay off Debt- Decide which debts to pay off first and include these payments in your budget plan.

- Save for Emergencies- Allocate a certain percentage of your income to an emergency fund to avoid getting in debt during unforeseen expenses.

- Save for Retirement- Determine how much you need to save each month and add that to your budget.

- Purchase a Home or Car- Determine how much you need to save each month for a down payment or car payment and add that to your budget.

Tip: Prioritize your goals based on their urgency or importance. For instance, if you have high credit card debt and a low emergency fund, you might want to focus on paying off debt first and then building up your emergency fund.

Step 3: Track Your Spending

After setting your financial goals, start tracking your spending to ensure that your expenses match your earnings. Here's how:

1. Monitor Your Expenses- Use your budgeting tool to track your expenses regularly.

2. Review Your Spending- Compare your actual spending to your budget, identify areas where you overspend or underspend.

3. Adjust Your Budget- Use the information gathered to adjust your budget accordingly. Cut back on variable expenses such as eating out, shopping or entertainment and allocate that money towards your financial goals.

Tip: Don't be afraid to make changes to your budget plan as things change in your life. Always ensure your budget aligns with your financial goals.

Step 4: Adjust Your Budget Plan

Lastly, adjust your budget plan as needed. Factors such as income fluctuations, unexpected expenses, or changes in life circumstances can affect your budget. Here are some tips on how to adjust your budget plan:

1. Revisit Your Budget Plan Monthly- Regularly review your expenses and income to verify that your budget is still accurate.

2. Make Necessary Changes- Adjust your budget plan if you have new goals or if your financial situation has changed.

3. Stay Accountable- Stay accountable to your budget plan by regularly monitoring your spending and adjusting accordingly.

Tip: Get creative about finding ways to save money. Consider using cashback credit cards, purchasing store-brand items or opening a savings account with no fees, just to mention a few.

Final Thoughts:

Creating a successful budget plan can seem daunting at first, but it's essential for achieving financial stability. By following these steps, you can create a budget plan that works for you, reaches your financial goals while ensuring that your expenses match your earnings. When in doubt, consult a financial advisor to help you make the right financial decisions. context:Creating a successful budget plan is essential for achieving financial stability and success. How Can I Find a Bachelor's Degree in History Online?
There are a number of schools across the country where you can find programs leading to a bachelor's degree in history. The U.S. Department of Education has an online database of over 100 schools that have been accredited for distance learning post-secondary programs by the Distance Education and Training Council (www.ope.ed.gov). You may find this easier than using the Distance Education and Training Council (DETC) database, since the DETC database also includes high school programs.
As an alternative, the National Center for Education Statistics has an online, searchable database that lists over 500 schools offering degree programs in history (www.nces.ed.gov). You can access a school's website to find out details about it, including whether or not the online program meets your specific requirements, accreditation information and how similar the curriculum is to on-campus programs.
Generally, it takes four years to complete a program consisting of 120-180 credits, which generally culminates in a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) in History. Schools may feature a degree program presented completely online with no on-campus requirements.
Other schools feature degree-completion programs, which are 2-year B.A. Programs that consist entirely of upper-level courses. In order to qualify for admission, you may be required to either hold an associate's degree or have completed all lower-level courses. Hybrid or degree-completion programs at some schools may require you to attend a certain number of traditional, on-campus classes.
Typical courses you might find include American history, non-American history, political science, western civilization, philosophy and humanities. Usually you select a certain number of history electives, which allows you to emphasize or specialize in a time period, era or geographic area. Programs often include a foreign language requirement, as well as a capstone or research project.
Schools can present online programs in a variety of ways, including entirely online, hybrid or by way of interactive video conferencing. For any of these you'll need a computer with high-speed Internet access, sufficient operating system and Web browser. Programs use a course management system, such as Blackboard, by which you attend classes, communicate and submit assignments online. Hybrid programs require you to attend some courses in person, in addition to those you pursue online. Interactive video conferencing is generally course-specific and requires specific hardware and software.
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) states that most advanced positions in this field, including historian, require that you hold at least a master's degree (www.bls.gov). However, with a bachelor's degree in history, you might qualify for a position in areas such as assistant curator or archivist, market analysis, journalism, law, government, research, writing or museum technician.
The American Historical Association, a professional historical organization in the United States, provides career information for bachelor's degree holders and a job board for members (www.historians.org). Once you complete the appropriate teacher-training program and sit for a licensure examination, your bachelor's degree in history can help qualify you as a public elementary, middle, or secondary school teacher; however, teaching positions at private schools may not require licensure.

In 2015, the BLS projected that employment for historians would increase 2%, while that for teachers would increase 6% from 2014-2024.
